new.title: Look up at the painted vault of Saint-Jacques
new.desc: Founded as a Benedictine abbey church in 1015 and rebuilt in Flamboyant Gothic in the 16th century, Saint-Jacques hides a fully painted net vault studded with carved keystones. Many call it the most beautiful church in Belgium.
new.tip: Entry is free; volunteer guides often give free tours, and from November to March the church hosts an organ festival under that same vault.

new.title: Find the Lucifer of Liège in Saint-Paul's
new.desc: Tucked under the pulpit of Saint-Paul's Cathedral sits Guillaume Geefs' marble 'Génie du mal', a chained, winged and strikingly handsome fallen angel. It replaced his brother's version, which the clergy removed for being far too seductive.
new.tip: Walk round to the back of the pulpit, at the foot of its twin staircases; the figure is easy to miss from the nave.

new.title: Explore the arms dealer's palace at the Grand Curtius
new.desc: The red-brick mansion of Jean Curtius, a 17th-century arms merchant, now holds Wallonia's biggest museum: Mosan treasures like the Évangéliaire de Notger, Val-Saint-Lambert crystal and one of the world's great collections of firearms.
new.tip: Combine it with Saint-Barthélemy and the Bueren steps; all three are a few minutes apart along Féronstrée and Hors-Château.

new.title: Step into Walloon life at the Cour des Mineurs
new.desc: The Musée de la Vie wallonne fills a former Friars Minor convent with everyday Wallonia from the 19th century to today, told through objects old and new across five themes on Walloon society, people, ideas and know-how.
new.tip: Entry to the permanent collection is free on the first Sunday of the month; the cloister courtyard itself is a quiet escape just behind Place du Marché.
new.q: Musée de la Vie wallonne Cour des Mineurs Liège

new.title: Duck under the arch into Impasse de la Couronne
new.desc: Rue Hors-Château is riddled with hidden cul-de-sacs where workers once lived and worked. Impasse de la Couronne, through a low beamed archway, opens onto cobbles, coloured shutters and a little green square facing the wooded citadel slopes.
new.tip: Look for number 41 on Hors-Château; once inside, the street noise simply disappears. Peek into the neighbouring impasses on the same side too.
new.q: Impasse de la Couronne Rue Hors-Château Liège

new.title: Meet the fish and fossils at the Aquarium-Muséum
new.desc: On the Outremeuse quay, the Aquarium-Muséum pairs living tanks with an old-style zoology museum. Together with the house of science next door, it is the most visited museum complex in Wallonia.
new.tip: A great rainy-day plan with children; the Maison de la Science is in the same building.
new.q: Aquarium-Muséum Quai Edouard Van Beneden Liège

new.title: Eat boulets at Café Lequet
new.desc: An old-school pub on the Meuse quay, Café Lequet is where many Liégeois send you for the city's best boulets-frites. Tête de veau is on the menu too, for the brave.
new.tip: No frills and often full; be ready to wait for a table, especially on Sunday after the Batte market across the river.
new.q: Café Lequet Quai sur Meuse 17 Liège

new.title: Find the hidden Pot au Lait
new.desc: At the back of a courtyard in Le Carré, this bar has been serving students and old regulars since 1979 amid wild murals, sculptures and odd objects. The mood shifts from café by day to party at night.
new.tip: You cannot see it from the street: walk into the courtyard at Rue Sœurs de Hasque 9.
new.q: Le Pot au Lait Rue Soeurs de Hasque Liège

new.title: Sing along at Aux Olivettes
new.desc: Aux Olivettes is a rare survivor of the cafés chantants of Jacques Brel's day: a pianist plays and regulars stand up to sing old French chansons for the room.
new.tip: Go late in the evening when the piano gets going; knowing the chorus of a Piaf song earns you instant friends.
new.q: Aux Olivettes Rue Pied du Pont des Arches 6 Liège

new.title: Drink a Curtius at Brasserie C
new.desc: Two agronomists brew the city's own beers in an impasse at the foot of the Bueren steps. Try the light, fruity Curtius or the coffee-dark Black C on terraces among terraced gardens.
new.tip: Perfect reward after climbing Bueren; in good weather head straight for the garden terraces up the slope.
new.q: Brasserie C Impasse des Ursulines 14 Liège

new.title: Hunt for treasure at the Saint-Pholien flea market
new.desc: Every Friday morning, stalls of vinyl, old ceramics and army surplus line Boulevard de la Constitution around Saint-Pholien church. It is smaller and far more local than the Sunday Batte.
new.tip: Come early, as it packs up around lunchtime; Simenon set his novel 'Le Pendu de Saint-Pholien' in these same streets.
new.q: Brocante de Saint-Pholien Boulevard de la Constitution Liège

new.title: Follow young Simenon through Outremeuse
new.desc: Georges Simenon, father of Inspector Maigret, grew up in Outremeuse and said Liège was in all his novels. A free app trail leads you past the houses, churches and streets of his youth, with audio stories at each stop.
new.tip: Download the 'Parcours Simenon' app before you go, then cross the Pont des Arches and let it guide you.

new.title: Warm up at the Village de Noël
new.desc: Started in 1986 with a handful of stalls around the Perron, Liège's Christmas village is now one of the biggest and oldest in Belgium, spreading over Place du Marché and Place Saint-Lambert with a Ferris wheel and a skating rink.
new.tip: Weekday evenings are far calmer than weekends; grab a hot pékèt and walk between the squares under the lights.
new.q: Village de Noël Place Saint-Lambert Liège

new.title: Wander the green Coteaux de la Citadelle
new.desc: Right above the old town, a web of footpaths runs through orchards, woods and terraced gardens on the citadel hill, with views over the rooftops and the Meuse. It feels like countryside five minutes from Place du Marché.
new.tip: Go up by the Bueren steps or Rue Pierreuse and come down through the Bois des Mineurs; the tourist office has a free route called 'Le sentier des terrasses'.

new.title: See a show in the old baths of La Cité Miroir
new.desc: The former public baths of Sauvenière have become La Cité Miroir, a cultural centre for exhibitions, talks, film screenings and performances in a striking old bathhouse building.
new.tip: Check the programme before you go; the Brasserie Sauvenière with its inner courtyard is just across the square.
new.q: La Cité Miroir Place Xavier Neujean Liège

new.title: Watch the fountains play at the Jardins d'Annevoie
new.desc: Laid out from 1758 near the Meuse south of Namur, these water gardens run their cascades, jets and canals on spring water alone, fed by the same streams that once drove the family's forges.
new.tip: Between Namur and Dinant; combine it with Freÿr or Dinant the same day. The gardens are a summer-season outing.

new.title: Watch climbers from the gardens of Freÿr
new.desc: On a bend of the Meuse south of Dinant, the Renaissance château of Freÿr and its 18th-century gardens, once visited by Louis XIV, face the limestone Rochers de Freÿr, Belgium's best-known climbing cliffs with hundreds of routes up to 120 metres.
new.tip: The château opens from spring to autumn, mostly Thursday to Sunday; bring binoculars to follow the climbers on the Al'Lègne face across the river.

new.title: See Li Rondia in the collegiate church of Huy
new.desc: The Collégiale Notre-Dame of Huy has the largest Gothic rose window in Belgium, known locally as Li Rondia and counted among the town's 'four wonders'. Its crypt keeps four gilded Mosan reliquaries from the 12th and 13th centuries.
new.tip: Huy is a short train ride up the Meuse from Liège; after the church, climb to the citadel for the view over the river.

new.title: Look down on the Tombeau du Géant near Bouillon
new.desc: North of Bouillon, the Semois loops almost completely around a wooded hill said to be a giant's grave. The viewpoint above it is the most photographed valley in the Ardennes.
new.tip: Drive or hike up to the Botassart viewpoint; late afternoon light in autumn is the classic shot.
new.q: Point de vue du Tombeau du Géant Botassart

new.title: Meet the Romans in Arlon
new.desc: Arlon was already a town in Roman times, and its archaeological museum has one of the finest Gallo-Roman sections in the country. Outside, a Roman tower and a copy of a Jupiter column found in 1972 keep the story going.
new.tip: Afterwards climb up to the Saint-Donat church on the hilltop; its tower looks out over Belgium, Luxembourg and France.

new.title: Hike to Reinhardstein castle and Belgium's highest waterfall
new.desc: Near Ovifat in the Hautes Fagnes, a medieval castle perched over the Warche gorge was rebuilt from its ruins in the late 1960s. Close by, the Reinhardstein waterfall is billed as the highest in Belgium.
new.tip: Park at Ovifat or by the Robertville dam and walk down through the forest; the path is steep and slippery after rain.

new.title: Climb to the castle ruins of La Roche-en-Ardenne
new.desc: The feudal ruins on their rocky spur above the Ourthe stand where a Celtic hill fort once was, and dominate one of the prettiest little towns of the Ardennes.
new.tip: Keep time for the Battle of the Ardennes museum in town, and for the Celtic ramparts of Le Cheslé, a short hike away.

new.title: Hear the roar of the Cascade de Coo
new.desc: The Amblève tumbles 15 metres at Coo, a waterfall partly man-made: in the 18th century the monks of Stavelot cut through a river bend to spare the village from floods.
new.tip: Coo has its own train station; take the chairlift up the hill next to the falls for a view over the whole valley.

new.title: Chew a biétrumé in Namur
new.desc: Namur's own sweet is a soft caramel of cooked cream, butter and roasted hazelnuts, created in 1954 and named after Biétrumé, a legendary local prankster.
new.tip: Look for them at the Maison des Desserts on Rue Haute-Marcelle, then nibble them on the way up to the citadel.
new.q: Maison des Desserts Rue Haute-Marcelle Namur

new.title: Buy jambon d'Ardenne in La Roche
new.desc: Ardennes ham, salted and smoked over wood, is the region's signature charcuterie. Boucherie Bouillon on the market square of La Roche-en-Ardenne has been making it, with dry-cured sausages, since 1955.
new.tip: Ask for a few slices cut thin and some sausage for a picnic by the Ourthe.
new.q: Boucherie Bouillon Place du Marché 9 La Roche-en-Ardenne

new.title: Toast with Maitrank in Arlon
new.desc: Maitrank, 'the May drink', is white Moselle wine steeped with sweet woodruff, sugar and orange slices. Arlon celebrates it every year at the Fêtes du Maitrank, the penultimate weekend of May.
new.tip: Outside the festival, local bars and shops sell it in spring; drink it well chilled with a slice of orange.

new.title: Eat tarte au riz in Verviers
new.desc: The creamy rice tart of the Liège region is claimed by Verviers, where the rice is slow-cooked in milk from the Herve plateau farms. Some bakers add a layer of crushed macaroon.
new.tip: Buy a slice at Darcis on Rue Crapaurue, then walk it off at the Centre Touristique de la Laine et de la Mode, in an old wool factory.

new.title: Taste Orval beer and cheese at the abbey
new.desc: In a valley near the French border, the Trappist abbey of Orval brews one of the world's most distinctive beers and makes its own cheese. Next to the new abbey lie the romantic ruins of the medieval one and the spring where Countess Mathilde found her lost ring.
new.tip: Visit the ruins and the cellar museum first, then sit down for an Orval with cubes of the abbey's cheese, the classic local pairing.

new.title: Taste Leffe where it began in Dinant
new.desc: Leffe beer takes its name from the Abbaye Notre-Dame de Leffe on the edge of Dinant, home to a religious community since 1152. Maison Leffe, by the Meuse, tells the story of the beer's origins and ends with a tasting.
new.tip: Walk on to the abbey itself, a short way north along the river, to see the abbey church.
new.q: Maison Leffe Charreau des Capucins Dinant

new.title: Get showered in confetti at the Laetare of Stavelot
new.desc: On the fourth Sunday of Lent, hundreds of Blancs Moussis in white hoods and long red noses take over Stavelot, mocking a prince-abbot's 1502 ban on monks joining the carnival. Cannons blast tonnes of confetti into the crowd.
new.tip: The big parade is on Sunday afternoon and ends with the Blancs Moussis' round dance on Place Saint-Remacle; expect confetti in your pockets for weeks.

new.title: Browse the bookshops of Redu
new.desc: This tiny Ardennes village turned itself into Belgium's village of books, with around two dozen second-hand bookshops and kilometres of shelves. On the first Saturday of August the Nuit du Livre ends with fireworks.
new.tip: Pair it with the Euro Space Center in neighbouring Transinne for a 'books and space' day.

new.title: Kayak down the Lesse to Anseremme
new.desc: The classic Ardennes summer outing: paddle down the Lesse from Houyet (21 km) or Gendron (12 km) to Anseremme near Dinant, through a quiet wooded valley.
new.tip: Leave the car at the finish and take the shuttle to the start. In dry spells the route can be shortened or closed, so check before you go.

new.title: Cycle the Vennbahn through the East Cantons
new.desc: The old Fagnes railway from Aachen to Troisvierges is now a long cycle path through the German-speaking East Cantons, past Raeren, Monschau, Waimes and Saint-Vith. The tracks are Belgian territory, which created little German enclaves on one side.
new.tip: Start at Raeren near Eupen and pedal south; on the stretch near Sourbrodt you can also try the Hautes Fagnes rail-bike.

new.title: Hop along the pools of the Ninglinspo
new.desc: The wildest little valley in Belgium: the Ninglinspo stream drops through a series of clear rock pools with names like the Bain de Diane and the Bain de Vénus, crossed by small footbridges.
new.tip: Park at Sedoz near Nonceveux (Aywaille) and follow the GR 15; wear good shoes, as the rocks are slippery.

new.title: Watch the stilt fighters at the Fêtes de Wallonie in Namur
new.desc: On the third weekend of September Namur throws its biggest party, with concerts, péket and folklore. The highlight is the échasseurs, stilt-walkers who battle each other on wooden stilts, a Namur tradition.
new.tip: Catch the stilt fighters' entrance on Place Saint-Aubain, and try the 'route du péket' boat trip between the town's locks.
